sheet.howExamined: P1 Higher tier only, 1 hour, 70 marks, calculator allowed. Velocity and acceleration are calculations worth [3] or [4]: [1] for the equation, [1] or [2] for the substitution, [1] for the answer, and on a slowing object [1] for the minus sign. traps: Treating speed and velocity, or distance and displacement, as the same quantity: the March 2026 Higher report found candidates unable to tell them apart (March 2026 P1 H Q5)
Missing that an object moving back towards its start is travelling in the opposite direction, so its velocity has the opposite sign (March 2026 P1 H Q5)
Finding an acceleration correctly and then not using a = (v − u) ÷ t to reach the final velocity; only a few managed it (March 2026 P1 H Q9)
Putting the wrong values of v, u and t into a = (v − u) ÷ t, including a final velocity divided by the time with the initial velocity left out (Summer 2023 P1 H Q7)
Using displacement = velocity × time with the final velocity when the velocity is changing, instead of the average velocity (Summer 2023 P1 H Q7)
Giving a slowing object a positive acceleration: final minus initial makes it negative, and the minus sign is a mark
Dividing by the time when rearranging for v: from a = (v − u) ÷ t, v − u = a × t

noteBlocks.lede: Some quantities need a direction as well as a size. Walk 400 m out and 100 m back and you have covered 500 m, yet you finish only 300 m from the start. This Higher-tier topic separates distance from displacement and speed from velocity, then builds acceleration, and retardation, from velocity.

noteBlocks.text: 1. Size only, or size and direction

noteBlocks.md:
A **scalar** has a size only. A **vector** has a size **and a direction**.
Each motion quantity comes in a pair, one of each kind, and the two share a unit. Force and weight are vectors too; mass, time and energy are scalars.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these quantities is a vector?
noteBlocks.explain: Displacement: how far, and in which direction, from the start. Distance and speed are sizes only.

noteBlocks.md:
**Displacement** is how far you finish from the start, in a stated direction: one straight arrow. On the walk, the distance is 500 m but the displacement is 300 m east.
Velocity comes from displacement as speed comes from distance:
**average velocity = displacement ÷ time**; in symbols, v = d ÷ t with d the displacement.
Over 250 s the walk's average speed is 2 m/s, but its average velocity is 1.2 m/s east.

noteBlocks.md:
Along a straight line there are only two directions, so a sign can carry the direction. Choose one direction as **positive**; the other is then **negative**.
With east positive, 15 m/s west is a velocity of **−15 m/s**. The speed is still 15 m/s: a speed never has a sign.

noteBlocks.title: Why bother with a sign?
noteBlocks.md: It is the shortest way to write a direction: the one character in −15 m/s does the work of the word west. The same sign will tell you, in the next section, when something is slowing down.

noteBlocks.explain: −6 m/s: the size is her speed, and the minus sign says west.

noteBlocks.md:
**Acceleration** is the change in velocity each second: **a = (v − u) ÷ t**, with u the initial velocity, v the final velocity and t the time taken. Its unit is **m/s²**. Always final minus initial.
**Worked example.** A train slows steadily from 24 m/s to 6 m/s in 12 s.
a = (6 − 24) ÷ 12 = **−1.5 m/s²**
The minus sign says it is slowing. A negative acceleration is a **retardation**: here, a retardation of 1.5 m/s². Many videos say **deceleration**; either earns the mark.

noteBlocks.prompt: A car slows steadily from 20 m/s to 8 m/s in 4 s. What is its acceleration, in m/s²?
noteBlocks.explain: (8 − 20) ÷ 4 = −3 m/s², a retardation of 3 m/s². A bare 3 would say the car was speeding up.

noteBlocks.md: When the velocity changes steadily, its average is halfway: **average velocity = (initial velocity + final velocity) ÷ 2**. Multiply by the time to get the displacement. Using the final velocity alone assumes it was reached at the very start, and gives an answer that is too big.

noteBlocks.prompt: A skater's velocity rises steadily from 2 m/s to 8 m/s in 4 s. What is her displacement in that time, in metres?

noteBlocks.md:
Say which quantities are vectors (size and direction) and which are scalars (size only), and pair them.
Tell distance from displacement and speed from velocity, and find average velocity = displacement ÷ time.
Use a sign for direction along a line, with one direction chosen as positive.
Calculate a = (v − u) ÷ t and call a negative acceleration a retardation.
Rearrange for a final velocity, and use the average of two velocities for a displacement.

This topic is Higher tier only. Expect a scalar-or-vector sort worth [1] each, then calculations worth [3] or [4]: the equation, the substitution and the answer, with a mark for the minus sign when something slows. The first mark is the equation; the last is the value with its sign. Stuck? Write a = (v − u) ÷ t, fill in the three values you know, and solve for the fourth.

Final minus initial, even though the final velocity is the smaller one.

options: Because a change is always the value after minus the value before
Because the bigger number always goes first
Because acceleration can never be negative
whyMenu.explain: After minus before is what a change means. When the bus slows, after is smaller, and the answer comes out negative on its own.

steps.decision: Keep the minus sign: it says the bus is slowing, and it is a mark of its own.

Substitute what you know first; rearranging with numbers is harder to get wrong than with letters.
Undo the division by multiplying both sides by the time, then add the starting velocity.

options: Because a × t is the velocity gained, which is added to the velocity it already had
Because acceleration and velocity have the same unit
Because the time must always be added
whyMenu.explain: Each second adds a metres per second; after t seconds that is a × t on top of u.

items.stem: Before we start (nothing here is new yet): what is 3 − 8?

options.feedback: A negative answer. Final minus initial gives exactly this when something slows down.
That is 8 − 3. Taking 8 from 3 goes below zero: −5.
That adds them. Taking 8 away from 3 gives −5.

items.stem: Before we start: in a = b ÷ c, which line makes b the subject?

options.feedback: Multiply both sides by c. The same move turns a = (v − u) ÷ t into v − u = a × t.
Dividing again would undo nothing. To remove '÷ c', multiply both sides by c.
That turns the equation upside down. Multiply both sides by c instead.

items.stem: Before we start: what is the unit of speed?

options.feedback: Metres per second. Velocity shares this unit.
That is the unit of a rate of change of speed. Speed itself is m/s.
Metres measure a distance. Speed is metres per second.

items.stem: Which of these is a vector quantity?

options.feedback: Velocity is speed in a stated direction.
Speed is velocity's scalar partner: a size only.
Distance is displacement's scalar partner: a size only.
That is the scalar partner of acceleration.

items.stem: A girl walks 70 m east along a straight path, then 30 m back west. What is her displacement from where she started?

options.feedback: 70 − 30 = 40 m, and she is still east of the start.
That adds the two legs: the distance she walked. Displacement is one arrow from start to finish.
The size is right, but she finishes east of the start, because she walked further east than west.

items.stem: A car slows steadily from 18 m/s to 6 m/s in 4 s. What is its acceleration?

options.feedback: (6 − 18) ÷ 4 = −3 m/s²: a retardation of 3 m/s².
Right size, wrong sign: a slowing car has a negative acceleration.
That divides the final velocity by the time. Use the change in velocity.
The velocities have been added. An acceleration uses final minus initial.

items.stem: A trolley moving at 5 m/s accelerates at 2 m/s² for 3 s. What is its final velocity?
items.skill: Final velocity from u, a and t

options.feedback: That is only the velocity gained. Add the velocity it already had.
The acceleration was divided by the time. Multiply them: a × t is the velocity gained.

items.stem: A lift's velocity rises steadily from 4 m/s to 10 m/s in 6 s. What is its displacement in that time?

options.feedback: Average velocity (4 + 10) ÷ 2 = 7 m/s, × 6 s = 42 m.
That uses the final velocity for the whole time. The lift only reached it at the end.
That halves the change in velocity. The average velocity adds the two velocities before halving.

Calculate the total distance the van moves.
hints: Distance ignores direction: every kilometre driven counts.

parts.stem:
A student walks from P to Q along the route shown, taking 8 minutes 20 seconds.
Calculate the size of the student's average velocity from P to Q.
Show your working out.

scheme.examinerNote: Physics papers print no equations, so the equation is recalled and written before any number goes in; a number put into a wrong equation scores nothing, even if it comes out right.

hints: Velocity uses the displacement: the straight line from P to Q, not the route.
Put the time into seconds first.
parts.workedSolution:
average velocity = displacement ÷ time
time = 8 × 60 + 20 = 500 s
average velocity = 1000 ÷ 500 = 2 m/s

commonErrors.feedback: 1400 m is the length of the route, a distance, so 1400 ÷ 500 is the average speed. Velocity uses the displacement, the dashed 1000 m: 1000 ÷ 500 = 2 m/s.
480 s is only the 8 minutes. Add the 20 s: 500 s, so the average velocity is 1000 ÷ 500 = 2 m/s.

parts.stem:
The student then walks back from Q to P along the same route.
State the student's displacement for the whole walk, there and back.
hints: Where does the walk finish, compared with where it started?
parts.workedSolution: Zero: the walk ends at P, where it started, so the straight line from start to finish has no length.

commonErrors.feedback: 2800 m is the distance walked there and back. The displacement is measured from start to finish, and both are at P: zero.

parts.stem: State the student's average velocity for the whole walk, there and back.
hints: Average velocity is displacement ÷ time.
parts.workedSolution: Zero: average velocity = displacement ÷ time, and the displacement for the whole walk is zero, however long it took.

context.setting: A train pulling away from a platform

parts.stem:
A train's velocity increases from 5 m/s to 29 m/s in 1 minute.
Calculate its acceleration.
Show your working out.

scheme.examinerNote: Physics papers print no equations, so the equation is recalled and written before any number goes in; a number put into a wrong equation scores nothing, even if it comes out right.

hints: The unit m/s² needs the time in seconds.
v is the final velocity and u the initial one.

commonErrors.feedback: That divides by 1, the time in minutes, giving m/s per minute. In seconds the time is 60 s: (29 − 5) ÷ 60 = 0.4 m/s².
That is the final velocity divided by the time. The train was already moving at 5 m/s, so only 29 − 5 = 24 m/s was gained. Summer 2023 examiners saw many substitute the wrong values of v and u.
The velocities have been added. An acceleration is the change: final minus initial, (29 − 5) ÷ 60 = 0.4 m/s².

context.setting: A car braking for a bend without stopping

parts.stem:
A car slows steadily from 26 m/s to 8 m/s in 4 s.
Calculate its acceleration.
Show your working out.

scheme.examinerNote: Physics papers print no equations, so the equation is recalled and written before any number goes in; a number put into a wrong equation scores nothing, even if it comes out right.
CCEA schemes give the minus sign of a negative acceleration its own mark.

hints: Final velocity minus initial velocity: the car is slowing, so expect a negative answer.

commonErrors.feedback: The size is right, but the car is slowing, so its acceleration is negative: −4.5 m/s². Final minus initial gives the sign by itself, and the scheme gives the minus sign a mark of its own. You may describe it in words as a retardation of 4.5 m/s², but the answer line asks for the acceleration, so write −4.5.
That divides the final velocity by the time. The acceleration uses the change in velocity: 8 − 26 = −18 m/s, over 4 s.
The velocities have been added. An acceleration needs the change, final minus initial: (8 − 26) ÷ 4 = −4.5 m/s².

parts.stem: What name is given to a negative acceleration?
hints: The specification's word begins with 'retard'.
parts.workedSolution: Retardation, the specification's word. Deceleration means the same and is accepted.

context.setting: A cyclist speeding up along a flat cycle path

parts.stem:
A cyclist moving at 3 m/s accelerates at 0.8 m/s² for 5 s.
Calculate her final velocity.
Show your working out.

scheme.examinerNote: Either form of the equation earns the first mark.

hints: Velocity gained = acceleration × time.
Then add the velocity she already had.

commonErrors.feedback: 4 m/s is the velocity she gained. She was already moving at 3 m/s, so add it: 3 + 4 = 7 m/s.
The acceleration has been divided by the time. From a = (v − u) ÷ t, multiply both sides by t: v − u = a × t = 4 m/s, so v = 7 m/s.

context.setting: A car joining a dual carriageway

parts.stem:
A car accelerates at 1.5 m/s² from 12 m/s to 30 m/s.
Calculate the time this takes.
Show your working out.
hints: Rearrange a = (v − u) ÷ t so that t is on its own: t = (v − u) ÷ a.

commonErrors.feedback: The change in velocity has been multiplied by the acceleration. The time is how many seconds it takes to gain 18 m/s at 1.5 m/s each second: 18 ÷ 1.5 = 12 s.
30 ÷ 1.5 is the time to reach 30 m/s from rest. The car started at 12 m/s, so it only has to gain 18 m/s: 12 s.

parts.stem:
A sprinter accelerates steadily from rest to 9 m/s in 3 s, running in a straight line.
Calculate her displacement in this time.
Show your working out.
hints: From rest means an initial velocity of 0 m/s.
Average the two velocities, then multiply by the time.
parts.workedSolution:
average velocity = (0 + 9) ÷ 2 = 4.5 m/s
displacement = average velocity × time = 4.5 × 3 = 13.5 m

commonErrors.feedback: That multiplies her final velocity by the time, as if she had left the blocks at 9 m/s. She started from rest, so use the average velocity, 4.5 m/s: 4.5 × 3 = 13.5 m. Summer 2023 examiners saw displacement = velocity × time used for a changing velocity.

context.setting: A train running east between two stations on a straight track

parts.stem:
A train leaves a station, travelling east along a straight track. Its velocity increases steadily from rest to 16 m/s in 40 s.
Calculate its acceleration.
Show your working out.

scheme.examinerNote: Physics papers print no equations, so the equation is recalled and written before any number goes in; a number put into a wrong equation scores nothing, even if it comes out right.

hints: From rest: u = 0 m/s.

parts.stem:
Calculate the train's displacement during these 40 s.
Show your working out.
hints: The velocity is changing, so the displacement needs the average velocity, not the final one.

commonErrors.feedback: 16 × 40 assumes the train was at 16 m/s all the way. It started from rest, so use the average velocity, 8 m/s: 8 × 40 = 320 m. Summer 2023 examiners named exactly this: displacement = velocity × time for a changing velocity.

parts.stem:
Approaching the next station, the train slows steadily from 16 m/s to 6 m/s in 25 s.
Calculate its acceleration during this time.
Show your working out.
hints: Slowing down while moving east: the acceleration points west, so it is negative.

commonErrors.feedback: The size is right, but the train is slowing, so the acceleration is −0.4 m/s²: a retardation. The minus sign is a mark of its own, and final minus initial produces it without any extra thought.
That is the final velocity divided by the time. The acceleration needs the change: 6 − 16 = −10 m/s in 25 s.

parts.stem:
At the end of this time a passenger says the train's velocity is 6 m/s.
Explain why this does not fully describe the train's velocity.

accepted: velocity is a vector, so it needs a direction as well: 6 m/s east

scheme.for: velocity is a vector: it needs a direction (east)

hints: What does a velocity have that a speed does not?
parts.workedSolution: Velocity is a vector, so it needs a direction as well as a size: 6 m/s east. 6 m/s on its own is only the speed.

context.setting: A lifeguard's training swim out to a buoy and back

parts.stem:
A lifeguard swims 100 m out to a buoy in a straight line and swims straight back to the steps where she started.
Explain the difference between scalar and vector quantities, using the lifeguard's swim to compare distance with displacement and speed with velocity. Give the unit of each quantity you use.
Your written communication is marked here as well: answer in full sentences, in a sensible order, using the specification's own scientific terms.

indicativeContent.point: a scalar has a size (magnitude) only
a vector has a size and a direction
distance is a scalar and displacement is a vector, both measured in metres
speed is a scalar and velocity is a vector, both measured in m/s
the lifeguard swims a distance of 200 m
her displacement is zero because she ends where she started
so her average speed is not zero but her average velocity is zero

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: The comparison is the point: distance and speed describe how far and how fast the lifeguard swam, displacement and velocity describe where she ended up. A point contradicted elsewhere is not counted.

hints: Define the two kinds of quantity first, then apply each pair to the swim.
There and back: add for the distance, then ask where she finished for the displacement.
parts.workedSolution: A scalar quantity has a size only, while a vector quantity has a size and a direction. Distance is a scalar and displacement is a vector, and both are measured in metres. Speed is a scalar and velocity is a vector, and both are measured in metres per second, m/s. The lifeguard swims 100 m out and 100 m back, so she swims a distance of 200 m. She finishes back where she started, at the steps, so her displacement is zero. Her average speed is the 200 m divided by her time, which is not zero, but her average velocity is her zero displacement divided by the time, so her average velocity is zero.

findTheMistake.stem:
Aoife is asked: 'A car moving at 12 m/s accelerates at 2.5 m/s² for 4 s. Calculate its final velocity. [3]'
Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 2 are right: the equation, with the numbers in the right places. Line 3 undoes the division the wrong way. To remove '÷ 4' from the right-hand side, both sides are multiplied by 4, so v − 12 = 2.5 × 4 = 10 m/s.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two of the three marks are already earned by lines 1 and 2, which is why the equation and the substitution are always worth writing. The March 2026 Higher report found most candidates could get an acceleration but few could use a = (v − u) ÷ t to reach a final velocity. A quick check helps: speeding up for 4 s at 2.5 m/s² must add far more than a fraction of 1 m/s.

prompts.answer: A vector has a size and a direction; a scalar has a size only.

prompts.prompt: Name the vector partner of distance, of speed and of rate of change of speed.

prompts.answer: v = d ÷ t: the average velocity is the displacement divided by the time taken.

prompts.prompt: Write the equation for acceleration in symbols, and say what each letter means.
prompts.answer: a = (v − u) ÷ t: v is the final velocity, u the initial velocity and t the time taken.

prompts.prompt: What is a negative acceleration called?

prompts.answer: v = u + a × t: multiply the acceleration by the time, then add the initial velocity.

prompts.answer: Both are zero, even though the distance walked and the average speed are not.
